questions.q: A 45-year-old man with CML has the Philadelphia chromosome in marrow cells but not in skin fibroblasts. How is this abnormality best described?

options.e: Wrong. A germline mutation would be present in all body cells and transmissible.
Wrong. The Philadelphia chromosome involves chromosomes 9 and 22, not 11 and 22.
Wrong. It is not inherited, and the breakpoints are reversed.
Correct. It is acquired, present in blood or marrow cells only, and not transmitted to offspring.

questions.q: A man homozygous for a 32-bp deletion in CCR5 remains uninfected despite repeated HIV exposure. What explains this?

options.t: His cells overproduce the CCR5 receptor
options.e: Wrong. A deletion would not cause overproduction.

options.t: His CCR5 protein is abnormally elongated
options.e: Wrong. Elongation is typical of stop-loss mutations, not this deletion.

options.t: The deletion is present only in his T cells
options.e: Wrong. It is a germline variant present in all cells.

options.t: His cells lack the CCR5 receptor
options.e: Correct. Without the receptor, HIV cannot enter the cell; this is a protective mutation.

questions.q: A 6-year-old with dry, scaly skin and extensive freckling burns after minimal sun exposure. Which UV-induced lesion is inadequately repaired in this disorder?

options.e: Wrong. UV causes dimers between adjacent pyrimidines, not purines.
Wrong. Mismatches are repaired by mismatch repair, not by nucleotide excision repair.
Correct. In xeroderma pigmentosum nucleotide excision repair fails to remove pyrimidine dimers.
Wrong. UV radiation does not mainly produce double-strand breaks here.

questions.q: Which of the following substitutions is a transition?

options.e: Wrong. Purine to pyrimidine is a transversion.
Wrong. Purine to pyrimidine is a transversion.
Wrong. Pyrimidine to purine is a transversion.
Correct. Purine for purine (A to G or G to A), or pyrimidine for pyrimidine, is a transition.

questions.q: The codon UCA (serine) changes to UCG (serine). What type of mutation is this?

options.e: Wrong. A missense change alters the amino acid, for example UCA to UUA (Ser to Leu).
Correct. The same amino acid is encoded, usually due to third-position degeneracy of the code.
Wrong. A nonsense change creates a stop codon, for example UCA to UGA.
Wrong. A frameshift needs an insertion or deletion not divisible by three.

questions.q: The codon UCA (serine) changes to UGA. What is the effect?

options.t: Missense mutation to a different amino acid
options.e: Wrong. UGA does not code for an amino acid.
Correct. UGA is a stop codon; mRNA is often degraded by nonsense-mediated decay.
Wrong. Serine is no longer encoded.

options.t: Stop-loss mutation giving an elongated chain
options.e: Wrong. Stop-loss occurs when a normal stop codon is mutated.

questions.q: A patient has sickle cell disease due to GAG to GTG in the beta-globin gene. How is this mutation classified?

options.t: Nonsense; glutamic acid replaced by a stop
options.e: Wrong. No stop codon is created.
Wrong. The amino acid does change.

options.t: Missense; valine replaced by glutamic acid
options.e: Wrong. The direction is reversed.

options.t: Missense; glutamic acid replaced by valine
options.e: Correct. Glutamic acid (two carboxyl groups) is replaced by valine (one), changing charge.

questions.q: Cystic fibrosis due to CFTR G542X results from which kind of mutation?

options.e: Correct. G542X means glycine at position 542 is replaced by a stop signal.
Wrong. A missense change would show a second amino acid, as in G551D.
Wrong. In-frame deletion is Phe508del.
Wrong. No loss or gain of nucleotides is implied by G542X.

questions.q: Which description fits CFTR p.Phe508del?

options.t: Frameshift deletion of one base pair
options.e: Wrong. A one-base deletion would disrupt the frame.
Wrong. Nonsense is typified by G542X.

options.t: In-frame deletion of three base pairs removing phenylalanine
options.e: Correct. Three adjacent base pairs are lost at codon 508, preserving the reading frame.

options.t: In-frame insertion of three base pairs
options.e: Wrong. It is a deletion, not an insertion.

questions.q: A boy has severe progressive muscle weakness from a dystrophin deletion that disrupts the reading frame. A different deletion in another patient is in-frame and causes milder disease. Which pair is correct?

options.e: Correct. Becker's downstream amino acid sequence is largely normal, explaining the milder phenotype.
Wrong. This reverses the pair.

options.t: Both are Duchenne; severity differs by deletion size only
options.e: Wrong. Reading frame, not size, decides severity.

options.t: Both are Becker; severity differs by deletion size only
options.e: Wrong. Reading frame decides severity.

questions.q: Which deletion would be expected to cause a frameshift?

options.e: Wrong. A multiple of three preserves the frame.
Correct. A number not divisible by three disrupts the frame, often giving a premature stop downstream.
Wrong. A multiple of three preserves the frame.
Wrong. A multiple of three preserves the frame.

questions.q: Hemoglobin Constant Spring has an elongated alpha chain. Which mutation type explains this?

options.e: Wrong. Nonsense shortens the chain by premature termination.

options.t: Stop-loss mutation in the termination codon (codon 142)
options.e: Correct. Mutating the stop codon gives an elongated chain.
Wrong. Not the mechanism described for Constant Spring.
Wrong. A silent mutation would not alter chain length.

questions.q: A fetus dies in utero with massive edema, heart failure and severe anemia. Absence of alpha chains is found. What is the usual molecular basis?

options.t: Point mutation in the beta-globin gene
options.e: Wrong. This causes beta-chain disease such as sickle cell disease.
Wrong. This is a mechanism for beta-thalassemia.
Wrong. Repeat expansions cause Fragile X, Huntington and myotonic dystrophy.
Correct. Alpha-thalassemia is mostly due to deletions from unequal crossover; the severe form causes hydrops fetalis.

questions.q: Achondroplasia due to FGFR3 G380R (rhizomelic shortening, large head, frontal bossing, normal intelligence) is an example of which mutational mechanism?

options.e: Wrong. This reduces or abolishes product, as in CFTR.
Correct. Increased expression or new function of FGFR3 produces the phenotype.
Wrong. This is half-normal product from a loss-of-function allele, e.g. familial hypercholesterolemia.
Wrong. This is a mutant product interfering with the normal allele, e.g. collagen.

questions.q: A heterozygous mutation in a collagen gene produces a mutant chain that interferes with the normal chains, causing osteogenesis imperfecta. Which mechanism is this?

options.e: Wrong. Here half the product is simply insufficient; the mutant does not interfere.
Wrong. This implies increased activity, as in FGFR3.
Correct. Common in dimers and multimers such as collagens.

options.t: Loss of function in the homozygous state only
options.e: Wrong. Disease occurs in the heterozygote.

questions.q: A patient has raised cholesterol without symptoms but a high risk of premature coronary artery disease; homozygous relatives have xanthomata. Which mechanism explains the heterozygote's phenotype?

options.e: Correct. Half the normal gene product is not enough; homozygotes are more severely affected.
Wrong. No interference by a mutant product is described.
Wrong. Activity is reduced, not increased.
Wrong. This produces an elongated protein and is unrelated.

questions.q: Which pairing of deletion syndrome and locus is correct?

options.e: Correct. Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary abnormalities, retardation.
Wrong. Williams is 7q11; 22q11.2 is DiGeorge.
Wrong. DiGeorge is 22q11.2.
Wrong. Wolf-Hirschhorn is 4p.

questions.q: A child has supravalvular aortic stenosis, peripheral pulmonary stenosis, a full lower lip, and is very outgoing. Which deletion is likely?

options.e: Wrong. DiGeorge: outflow tract defects, thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia, cleft palate.
Wrong. WAGR: Wilms tumor, aniridia.
Correct. This is Williams syndrome.
Wrong. Wolf-Hirschhorn: severe learning difficulties, failure to thrive.

questions.q: A newborn has a cardiac outflow tract malformation, hypocalcemia from parathyroid hypoplasia and absent thymus. Which deletion is responsible?

options.e: Correct. DiGeorge syndrome: heart malformations, thymic and parathyroid hypoplasia, cleft palate.
Wrong. Williams syndrome.
Wrong. WAGR syndrome.
Wrong. Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.

questions.q: A deletion involving loss of part of a chromosome results in which of the following?

options.e: Wrong. Trisomy needs extra material, as in duplication.
Wrong. Deletion removes material, so it is unbalanced.
Correct. Loss of part of a chromosome gives monosomy for the segment.
Wrong. Triploidy is a whole extra haploid set.
